observations: Two large circular eye forms dominate the upper half, each filled with radiating purple lines converging on a white oval center; the left circle is noticeably larger than the right.
A wide rectangular mouth sits in the lower third, its interior filled with closely spaced diagonal white and grey lines, framed by heavy dark outlines.
Diagonal pale beams cross the dark teal and grey face from upper corners, while loose multicolored lines—blue, red, yellow, green—layer across the edges and cheeks.
reading: The face fills the frame with little margin at the edges. The radiating purple eyes—wide, asymmetric in size, locked open—read as alarm or fixation. Diagonal light beams cut across the dense layered lines without resolving the tension they create. The row of teeth below adds a held-breath quality, somewhere between a grimace and a scream.
contextAngle: Within the owned nifty-faces subset, this work sits between title neighbors #87 and #89. Where #87 uses a warm yellow field and naturalistic proportions, #88 pushes toward near-abstraction with symmetrical circular eyes and a darker, cooler ground.

connections.reason: Both show an open-mouthed face with visible teeth and layered loose lines, but #87 sits on a bright yellow ground with warm tones while #88 replaces that warmth with dark teal and cool greys.

nnotb #134 shares a dark background, dense overlapping colored lines, and an open mouth with teeth, but its face tilts and scatters lines outward while #88 holds a frontal, near-symmetrical lock on the viewer.

lookingQuestion: The two eye circles are visibly different in size—what does that asymmetry do to the sense of balance across the otherwise near-symmetrical face?
ambiguities: The pale diagonal beams may be a background element or an overlay; their relationship to the face structure is not fully resolved in the image.
Candidate #89 shows a more architectural head with flat color zones and parallel line backgrounds—no strong formal parallel to #88 beyond a shared teeth motif, so it was omitted.
